title: Variables: let, const and var
summary: A variable is a name for a value. The name lets you use the value again later in your program.
introduction: A variable is a name for a value. The name lets you use the value again later in your program. Keep track of a score or a player name. Learn when to use let for a value that changes and const for a name you will not reassign.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with let and const and choose between them
Explain why const does not make an object or array unchangeable
Predict where a variable is visible using block scope
Describe the hoisting behaviour that makes var risky

blocks.text: A variable is a named container for a value. Without one you would have to repeat the value everywhere, and changing it would mean editing every copy. With a variable you write the value once, refer to it by name, and update it in one place. Declaring a variable also tells the reader what the value *means*: `taxRate` says more than `0.25`.
let: a value that can change

`let` declares a variable whose value may be replaced later. The first assignment is part of the declaration; after that you assign a new value with `=` and no keyword. The right-hand side can use the current value, which is how counters and running totals work.
The last line uses a **template literal**: text in backticks where `${...}` inserts a value. It is the easiest way to combine text and variables, and later lessons use it constantly.
const: a name that always points to the same value

`const` declares a variable that cannot be reassigned. Use it by default: most values in a program are set once, and a `const` tells readers (and the browser) that the name will not change. Trying to reassign one stops the script with an error.

blocks.text: `const` protects the *binding* (the link between the name and the value), not the value itself. An object or array stored in a `const` can still be modified from the inside; only replacing it with a completely different object is forbidden.

A **block** is anything between curly braces: the body of an `if`, a loop or a function. Variables declared with `let` or `const` exist only inside the block where they are declared. That is called **block scope**, and it means a temporary variable inside a loop cannot leak out and clash with another one of the same name.

Before 2015 the only keyword was `var`. It still works, but it has two behaviours that cause bugs. First, `var` ignores blocks: a variable declared inside an `if` is visible in the whole function. Second, `var` declarations are **hoisted**: the browser moves them to the top of the function, so you can read the variable before the line that declares it and get `undefined` instead of an error. `let` and `const` are also hoisted, but they stay unusable until their declaration runs, which turns the same mistake into a clear `ReferenceError`.

blocks.text: The `try`/`catch` wrapper lets the script continue after the error so you can see its name; the [Errors and Debugging](/tutorials/javascript/errors-debugging) lesson explains it fully. The lesson to take from this example: use `const` by default, `let` when a value must change, and `var` only when maintaining old code.

items: Names may contain letters, digits, `_` and `$`, but cannot start with a digit: `item2` is fine, `2items` is not.
Names are case-sensitive: `total`, `Total` and `TOTAL` are three different variables.
Reserved words such as `let`, `if`, `for` and `class` cannot be used as names.
By convention, use **camelCase** for variables and functions (`firstName`, `maxRetries`) and start class names with a capital letter (`ShoppingCart`).
Choose names that say what the value is: `remainingSeconds` beats `rs`.

blocks.title: Forgetting the keyword
blocks.text: Writing `total = 5;` without `let` or `const` does not declare a variable. In old-style scripts it silently creates a global variable that any other script can overwrite; in modules and strict mode it throws `ReferenceError: total is not defined`. Always declare a variable before you use it.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: In the block-scope example, change the outer `const level` to `let level` and the inner `const level = "inner"` to `level = "inner"` (no keyword). Run it again and explain to yourself why the second line of output changes.

questions.question: Which keyword should you reach for first when declaring a variable in modern JavaScript?
questions.explanation: Use const by default; switch to let only when the value must be reassigned. var has function scope and hoisting surprises, so it is reserved for old code.

questions.question: After `const list = [1, 2];`, the statement `list.push(3);` throws an error.
questions.explanation: const prevents reassigning the name, not changing the array it points to. push modifies the existing array, so it works; `list = []` would be the error.

seo.title: JavaScript Variables – let, const, var and Scope
seo.description: Learn how to declare JavaScript variables with let and const, why var is avoided, and how block scope and hoisting decide where a variable can be used.
